"A simple cache returns None both for a missing key and for a key that maps to None."

No, it returns KeyError. Or at least it should.
So much trouble to avoid introducing the optional monad.

When I was writing a bunch of Lua, I was a big fan of having a None sentinel value (Lua uses 'nil' for representing absence) and it was useful for a lot of things similar to Pydantic's MISSING.

This distinction is something that I think is actually handy about JavaScript, and distinguishing between 'null' and 'undefined' is sometimes useful for similar reasons.
I like it. I can't see how to do better while remaining compatible with Python idioms.

Here is the sample code from the article:

    > MISSING = sentinel("MISSING")

    > def update_email(user_id: int, email: str | None | MISSING = MISSING) -> None:
    >     if email is MISSING:
    >         return  # nothing to update
    >     elif email is None:
    >         db.delete_email(user_id)
    >     else:
    >         db.set_email(user_id, email.lower())  # narrowed to str
I see this style frequently from long time Python programmers. The language is so dynamic that people begin to think this is a good way to program. Hot take: It is not. Why not two different functions called delete_email() and set_email()? That would be more clear.

I hate sentinel values. Even/especially with AI-generated code.

1. If your date does not have a value, do not return 0, an empty string, or None. Use a discriminated union and model your domain rigorously.

2. If your data model accepts None/undefined as a value, that should translate to your business model as well. For example

3. Do not make your `name` field as `string | undefined` just because there might be an intermediate loading or processing state. It's better to model that as something like `Loaded` where Loaded is something like a Result or Optional type (though ideally more rigorously defined)
